text: With a rich history in foundry operation, they invented the AMEC process as a way to decrease the time and lower the cost to develop complex metallic geometries. In 2023, Skuld was selected as part of the Innovation Crossroads Cohort 2023. This gave them the opportunity to partner with researchers at ORNL to further develop the AMEC process via CRADA. The CRADA between ORNL and Skuld had four primary tasks: AMEC process improvements, computational model development, process and application window, and material characterization and qualification. Process improvements included slicing and toolpathing, alternative polymers, and alternative slurry coatings. The basic computational model was for developing a fundamental simulation model to represent how the AMEC process works for various input geometries. The process and application window was focused on qualifying the capabilities and testing new applications. Lastly, the material characterization and qualification task was about understanding the material performance of cast specimens. Ultimately, this project focused on testing, qualifying, and improving the AMEC process to prove commercial viability. 1.2 TECHNICAL RESULTS 1.2.1 AMEC Process Improvements The AMEC process starts with 3D printing a model of the desired cast geometry. Because the 3D printed model will be vaporized by the molten metal, it’s beneficial to minimize the amount of polymer used to make the 3D printed model. This is primarily done by printing thin walls, minimizing solid surfaces, and reducing infill to the lowest percentage possible. An additional opportunity is to perforate the surface or make many small holes in the surface. This minimizes the polymer used and also creates a path for gases to escape during vaporization. While parts can be perforated during design, this doesn’t translate well to toolpath generation for 3D printing. Instead, it’s best to add the functionality during or after slicing. Initially it was planned to implement this functionality to the ORNL Slicer software package, but a faster and simpler solution was developed in the form of a post-processor. This takes a g- code file as an input, allows the user to define settings for how the perforation works, and outputs a g- code file with small holes in the surface. The polymer used for 3D printing in the AMEC process is PLA (polylactic acid); a material made from corn. PLA has a low melting point and was found to only take approximately 15 seconds to fully vaporize when testing with the TGA (thermogravimetric analysis). This TGA was used to determine how the PLA performed when ramping temperature at a maximum speed of 500C. Testing was conducted with a variety of PLA materials to understand if and how colorant impacted the burn off. Natural PLA, with no colorant, left no material behind after vaporizing. White, which typically requires the most colorant to manufacture, left the largest amount of residual material behind (approximately 6.4% of the starting weight) as shown in Figure 1. In comparison foams such as expanded polystyrene (EPS) and extruded polystyrene (XPS) leave no remnants behind.
